readings.c1s1:
that may be implicitly confided in: applied to persons: as, a ''trusty'' servant.
{{smaller block|Use careful watch, choose ''trusty'' sentinels.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., v. 3. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' Not liable to fail; that may be relied upon, as in an emergency; strong; firm: applied to things: as, a ''trusty'' sword.
{{smaller block|<poem>The neighing steeds are to the chariots tied,
The ''trusty'' weapon sits on every side.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vii. 886.}}}}
'''3†.''' Trusting; trustful.
{{smaller block|<poem>He [who is born under Mercury] wilbe (soe his state thereby may mend)
Apt to deceive even his most ''trusty'' friend.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 115.}}}}
'''4.''' Involving trust and responsibility. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It were fit you knew him, lest . . . he might at some great and ''trusty'' business in a main danger fail you.
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iii. 6. 16.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''trusties'' (-tiz). A trusty person; specifically, a well-behaved and trustworthy convict to whom special privileges are granted.
{{smaller block|By far the greater number of criminals confined in the jails of the far West are there for a class of offenses peculiar to the country. They are men dangerous in one direction, perhaps, but generally not depraved. The ''trusties'' are often domesticated upon ranches near the town, and apparently are unwatched, and on the best of terms with the ranchman’s family. ''The Century'', XXXVII. 448.}}

'''trut''', ''interj.'' [ME. ''trut'', also ''ptrupt'', ''ptrot'', < OF. ''trut'', an interj. of contempt. Cf. ''tut''<sup>4</sup>.] An interjection of contempt. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 415.

'''truth''' (tröth), ''n.'' [Also, in a form now differentiated, ''troth'', q. v.; < ME. ''truthe'', ''treuthe'', ''trewthe'', ''trewwethe'', ''treouthe'', ''treowthe'', etc., also ''trouthe'',
readings.c2s3:
¶
{{smaller block|''Truthiness'' is a habit, like every other virtue. There I hold by the Peripatetics. ''Noctes Ambrosianæ'', Feb., 1832.}}

'''truthless''' (tröth′les), ''a.'' [< ''truth'' + ''-less.'' Cf. ''trothless.''] '''1.''' Lacking truth; lacking reality; untrue.—'''2.''' Faithless.
{{smaller block|<poem>Cast all your eyes
On this—what shall I call her?—''truthless'' woman!</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, v. 1.}}}}

'''truthlessness''' (tröth′les-nes), ''n.'' The character of being truthless.

'''truth-lover''' (tröth′luv″ėr), ''n.'' One devoted to the truth.
{{smaller block|<poem>Truth-teller was our England’s Alfred named;
''Truth-lover'' was our English Duke.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Death of Wellington, vii.}}}}

'''truthness†''' (tröth′nes), ''n.'' Truth. ''Marston.'' [Rare.]

'''truth-plight†''' (tröth′plīt), ''v.'' [< ME. ''truthplyten'', ''truplyten''; < ''truth'' + ''plight''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''troth-plight.''] To pledge one’s faith; betroth; affiance. ''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 504.

'''truth-teller''' (tröth′tel″ėr), ''n.'' One who tells the truth. See the quotation under ''truth-lover.''

'''truth-writ''' (tröth′rit), ''a.'' Truthfully written. ''George Eliot.'' [Rare.]

'''truthy''' (trö′thi), ''a.'' [< ''truth'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Truthful; veracious. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|They would have a more ''truthy'' import than what at present they convey.
{{right|''W. G. Palgrave'', Central and Eastern Arabia, I. ix.}}}}

''truthe'', ''treuthe'', ''trewthe'', ''trewwethe'', ''treouthe'', ''treowthe'', etc., also ''trouthe'', trowthe, < AS. ''treówthu'', ''treówth'' (''treówth-'', ''treóth-'') (= OHG. *''triuwida'', in comp., = Icel. ''tryggth''), truth, faith; with formative ''-th'', < ''treówe'', true: see ''true''.] '''1.''' The state or character of being true; trueness. {{smaller|(''a'') Conformity of thought with fact; conformity of a judgment, statement, or belief with the reality; exact correspondence of subjective and objective relations.}} {{smaller block|All admit that by ''truth'' is understood a harmony, an agreement, a correspondence between our thought and that which we think about. This definition we owe to the schoolmen. “Veritas intellectus,” says Aquinas, “est adæquatio intellectus et rei, secundum quod intellectus dicit esse quod est, vel non esse quod non est.” {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton'', Logic, xxvii.}}}} {{smaller block|In common life we call ''truth'' the agreement between an object and our conception of the object. We thus presuppose an object to which our conception must conform. In the philosophical sense of the word, on the other hand, ''truth'' may be described, in a general and one-sided way, as the agreement of the subject-matter of thought with itself. {{right|''Hegel'', Logic (tr. by Wallace), p. 43.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') The state of being made true or exact; exact conformity to a model, rule, or plan; accuracy of adjustment; exact adaptation.}} {{smaller block|Ploughs, to go true, depend much on the ''truth'' of the iron-work. {{right|''Mortimer'', Husbandry.}}}} {{smaller block|Most gun-stocks are twisted over — that is to say, the toe of the butt is more out of ''truth'' with the barrels than the heel. {{right|''W. W. Greener'', The Gun, p. 432.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') In the ''fine arts'', the proper and correct representation of any object in nature, or of whatever subject may be under treatment; specifically, in ''arch.'', avoidance of deceits in construction or decoration, as of non-concordance of apparent and real structure, or of imitation of stone or marble in paint or plaster.}} {{smaller block|The agony of the Laocoon, the action of the Discobulus, the upspringing of the Mercury, are all apparently real in their action by the innate ''truth'' of their conformation. . . . ''Truth'' is therefore the highest quality in Art. {{right|''Fairholt'', Dict. Terms of Art.}} In ''truth'' and skill of modelling even the sculptures of Chartres and St. Denis, which are a century earlier in date, surpass those of Wells. {{right|''C. H. Moore'', Gothic Architecture, p. 286.}}}} (''d'') Habitual disposition to speak only what is true; veracity; purity from falsehood; truthfulness; sincerity; uprightness; honesty: as, a man of ''truth.'' {{smaller block|For als longe as zee ben bounden to gedere in places — that is to seyne, in Love, in ''Trouthe,'' and in gode Accord — no man schalle ben of powere to greve zou. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 229.}} Love is all ''truth.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 804.}}}} (''e'') Disposition to be faithful; fidelity; constancy. {{smaller block|Long since we were resolved of your ''truth.'' {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 4. 20.}} Now I shall try thy ''truth.'' If thou dost love me, Thou weigh’st not any thing compar’d with me. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, ii. 1.}} Alas! they had been friends in youth; But whispering tongues can poison ''truth.'' {{right|''Coleridge'', Christabel, ii.}}}} (''f'') The state of not being counterfeited or adulterated; genuineness; purity. {{smaller block|The ''truth'' of thy love to me. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2. 13.}}}} '''2.''' That which is true. (''a'') Fact; reality; verity: as, a lover of ''truth'': often personified. {{smaller block|“Sygrem,” he seid, “to yow I will not leyne, I shall yow telle the ''trouth'' of this mater.” {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2284. ''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 332.}}}} {{smaller block|You peradventure think aptness and ableness all one; whereas the ''truth'' is that, had we kept our first ableness, grace should not need. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v., App. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|For my mouth shall speak ''truth''. {{right|Prov. viii. 7.}}}} For ''truth'' is ''truth'' To the end of reckoning.{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., v. 1. 45.}} Oh, ''Truth'', thou art a mighty conqueress!{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Queen of Corinth, iv. 3.}} {{smaller block|''Truth'' is the most unbending and uncompliable, the most necessary, firm, immutable, and adamantine thing in the world. {{right|''Cudworth'', Morality, IV. v. § 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Kant regards it as a duty owed to oneself to speak the ''truth'', because “a lie is an abandonment or, as it were, annihilation of the dignity of man.” {{right|''H. Sidgwick'', Methods of Ethics, p. 292.}}}} (''b'') A verified fact; a true statement or proposition; an established principle, fixed law, or the like. {{smaller block|Fundamental ''truths'', . . . like the lights of heaven, are not only beautiful and entertaining in themselves, but give light and evidence to other things that without them could not be seen. {{right|''Locke'', Conduct of the Understanding, § 43.}}}} (''c'') That which is righteous or in accordance with the divine standard. {{smaller block|He that doeth ''truth'' cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God. {{right|John iii. 21.}}}} '''3†.''' Faith pledged; pledge; troth. See ''troth''. I’ll give thee the ''truth'' of my right hand; The ''truth'' of it I’ll freely gie.{{right|''Young Beichan and Susie Pye'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 4).}} '''Cartesian criterion of truth.''' See ''Cartesian''.—'''Complex truth.''' See ''complex''.—'''Contingent truth,''' a truth which is not absolute, but contingent on something else.—'''Criterion of truth.''' See ''criterion''.—'''Ethical truth.''' See ''ethical''.—'''Fewness and truth†.''' See ''fewness''.—'''Formal, fundamental, gospel truth.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.}}—'''God’s truth.''' {{smaller|See ''God''1.}}—'''Immediate truths.''' {{smaller|See ''immediate'', 4.}}—'''In truth,''' {{smaller|truly; in fact; also, sincerely.}}—'''Logical, material, objective truth.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.}}—'''Of a truth, of truth,''' {{smaller|in truth; in reality; certainly.}} {{smaller block|Ffor ''of trewthe'' he ys not content with no man that ys famyliar with the company that ys at the Rodes, ffor that hell broude takys them as hys mortall enimies. {{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 22.}} ''Of a truth'' it is good to be with good people. {{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xxiii.}}}} '''Physical, pure, real, secondary, transcendental,''' {{smaller|etc.,}} '''truth.''' {{smaller|See the adjectives.}} ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|See ''reality''1.}} '''truth''' (tröth), ''v. t.'' [< ''truth'', ''n.''] To affirm or declare truthfully. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The ancients Who chatted of the golden age feigned trifles. Had they dreamt this, they would have ''truth’d'' it heaven. {{right|''Ford'', Fancies, ii. 2.}}}} '''truthful''' (tröth′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''truth'' + ''-ful''.] '''1.''' Full of truth; habitually speaking the truth; veracious. {{smaller block|The perfectly ''truthful'' man cannot entertain the proposal to say what is false. {{right|''J. Sully'', Outlines of Psychol., p. 666.}}}} '''2.''' Conformable to truth; correct; true: as, a ''truthful'' statement. ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Sincere, honest, candid, frank, open, ingenuous, artless, guileless.}} '''truthfully''' (tröth′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a truthful manner; with truth. '''truthfulness''' (tröth′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The character of being truthful: as, the ''truthfulness'' of a person or of a statement. ''tritare'', rub, thresh, freq. of L. ''terere'', pp. ''tritus'', rub, thresh: see ''trite''1.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To separate, as what is good from what is bad; separate by sifting; sift. {{smaller block|The wylde corne, beinge in shape and greatnesse lyke to the good, if they be mengled, with great difficultie wyll be ''tryed'' out. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, ii. 14.}}}} Hence—(''a'') To select; cull; pick out. The kinges sone aswithe let sembul miche puple, & ''triȝed'' him to a tidi ost of the tideȝist burnes. {{smaller block|{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3556.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') To ascertain by sifting or examination. ''Alisaunder of Macedoine'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 761.}} {{smaller block|Master More was once sent in commission into Kent, to help to ''try'' out, if it might be, what was the cause of Goodwin Sands. {{right|''Latimer'', Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}} '''2.''' To separate (metal) from the ore or dross by melting; refine; assay. [Not a technical use.] {{smaller block|Silver ''tried'' in a furnace of earth, purified seven times. {{right|Ps. xii. 6.}} The fire seven times ''tried'' this; Seven times ''tried'' that judgement is That did never choose amiss. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., ii. 9. 63.}}}} '''3.''' To separate or reduce by boiling or steaming; render: generally with ''out'': as, to ''try out'' lard or blubber. {{smaller block|Aysell and wyne eke ''oute'' of hem men ''trie''. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 53.}} ''Palm.'' All my fat Oxen and Sheep are melted to this [money], Gentlemen. ''Whead.'' Their Grease is well ''try’d'', Sir. {{right|''Etherege'', Love in a Tub, ii. 3.}}}} '''4.''' To put to the test or proof; subject to experimental treatment, comparison with a standard, or the like, in order to determine the truth, accuracy, power, strength, speed, fitness, or other quality of; test; prove: as, to ''try'' weights and measures; to ''try'' a new invention; to ''try'' conclusions; to ''try'' one’s patience, or one’s luck. {{smaller block|This word of God ''trieth'' all doctrine. {{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 9.}}}} {{smaller block|It is a true Observation that, among other effects of Affliction, one is to ''try'' a Friend. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 55.}} If God come to ''trie'' our constancy, we ought not to shrink, or stand the lesse firmly for that. {{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 7.}} Had we no other way of ''trying'' the continuance of God’s goodness to us but by exercising his patience by our greater provocations? {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. i.}} Your Goblin’s Skill shall now be ''try’d.'' {{right|''Congreve'', An Impossible Thing.}}}} '''5.''' To use, apply, or practise tentatively; experiment with: as, to ''try'' a new remedy; also, to experiment upon; treat tentatively. {{smaller block|A bulbe of sqylle eke summen wol devyde, And ther into this plannte of fig-tree ''trie'', And bynde it so therto that it abyde. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 124.}} He [a hare] was ill three days, during which time I nursed him, . . . and by . . . ''trying'' him with a variety of herbs restored him to perfect health. {{right|''Cowper'', Treatment of Hares.}} If that child were mine, Francis, I should ''try'' her with a little taraxacum. {{right|''Mrs. Annie Edwardes'', Ought we to Visit her? xi.}} The artist sometimes ''tried'' an attitude on a grouping, and then, dissatisfied with the effect, abandoned it. {{right|''Harrison and Verrall'', Ancient Athens, p. cxi.}}}} '''6.''' To endeavor experimentally to find out. {{smaller block|We are four damsels sent abroad, To the east, west, north, and south, To ''try'' whose fortune is so good To find these champions forth. {{right|''Robin Hood and the Stranger'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 412).}}}}
